questions.stem: Engineer Joe measures 5 cm on a 1:40000 map and must report the ground distance in kilometres.
questions.explanation: Five centimetres times forty thousand is two hundred thousand centimetres, or two kilometres.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A verbal scale and its equivalent fraction
questions.learningObjective: Compare verbal scales in a brief
questions.stem: Engineer Kim compares one centimetre to five hundred metres with one inch to the mile and states which is larger.

answer.exemplar: One centimetre to five hundred metres is 1:50000, while one inch to the mile is 1:63360, so the centimetre scale is larger and shows more detail.

questions.explanation: Converting both to representative fractions shows 1:50000 is larger than 1:63360, so the centimetre scale is the larger scale.

questions.explanation: Individual trees need fine resolution, which only a large scale such as 1:500 provides; smaller scales shrink trees to dots.

questions.stem: Engineer Nora reports that the Lambert conformal conic preserves.
questions.explanation: Lambert conformal conic preserves angles and local shapes, which is why it suits mid-latitude aviation charts.

questions.topic: Area error of a conformal projection at a stated latitude
questions.learningObjective: Compute area error at 30 degrees
questions.stem: Engineer Owen computes the Mercator area scale factor at 30 degrees latitude to two decimals.
questions.explanation: The linear scale factor is 1/cos30 = 1.1547, and squaring gives 1.333, or 1.33 to two decimals.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a conformal projection promises
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conformal claim in a brief
questions.stem: Engineer Pat evaluates a claim that a conformal projection is best for measuring land areas.

options.text: The claim is true only at the equator
The claim is false; use equal-area instead
The claim depends on the map colour

questions.explanation: Measuring land areas requires true area, so an equal-area projection is correct; conformal distorts area and is wrong for this task.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What an equal-area projection gives up
questions.learningObjective: Explain the equal-area tradeoff in a brief
questions.stem: Engineer Quinn explains in a brief what an equal-area projection gives up to keep area true.

answer.exemplar: An equal-area projection gives up true shape and true angles; regions away from the standard parallels are stretched or compressed so that their area remains correct.

questions.explanation: Area conservation forces shape and angle distortion, which is the tradeoff an equal-area projection accepts.

questions.learningObjective: Summarise the scale detail-extent tradeoff
questions.stem: Engineer Ugo summarises the relationship between scale, detail and extent for a client.

options.text: Large scale means large extent and low detail
Extent and detail are always equal
Scale does not affect detail or extent
Large scale means small extent and high detail

questions.explanation: Large scale enlarges features, raising detail but shrinking the area that fits on a sheet; small scale does the opposite.
